title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026]
Title:From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. Moreover, task outcomes and execution trajectories alone provide limited supervision for determining whether a subagent has received appropriate permissions. We observe that Agent Skills encode procedural knowledge describing the operations, tools, and files required at each step, providing a natural source of supervision for authorization. Building on this observation, we synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures from Skills, execute them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and use verified trajectories to construct training data for task execution and authorization. On ClawArena-Team, our method improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, while increasing overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

report.summary: Paper shows Agent Skills' step-by-step procedures can supervise training for precise subagent tool and workspace permissions, improving authorization precision and task success.
report.background: Multi-agent AI systems increasingly delegate specialized subtasks to subagents, each needing access to particular tools and workspace resources. Existing orchestration frameworks can restrict tools and execution environments, but they rarely specify the exact resources a delegated subtask requires. Overbroad permissions increase security and data-risk exposure, while overly narrow permissions cause task failures. Final task outcomes and execution traces provide weak supervision for judging whether a subagent received appropriate access. The paper observes that Agent Skills contain procedural knowledge: step-by-step descriptions of operations, tools, and files needed. It treats this as a natural supervision signal for learning precise subagent authorization.
key_points: The core problem is least-privilege authorization for delegated subagents. Current systems control tool access and sandboxes but do not directly encode which resources each subtask needs, and outcome-only supervision cannot reliably tell whether permissions were appropriate.

The method synthesizes tasks and step-by-step procedures from Agent Skills, executes them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and verifies trajectories. These verified traces become training data for both task execution and authorization decisions.

On ClawArena-Team, the approach improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points, workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, and overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.

The approach remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis methods on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, suggesting that procedural Skill knowledge offers dense supervision beyond final outcomes.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the work reframes agent authorization as a learnable capability rather than only a static policy layer, pointing toward orchestration platforms that infer least-privilege access per subtask. Developers can use procedural skills as specifications to generate permission-aware training data and policies, but should still combine learned authorization with deterministic enforcement and sandboxing. Regular users could see agents that complete complex tasks with fewer unnecessary permissions, reducing exposure of files, credentials, and tools. The main caveat is that learned permissions are not a substitute for audited policy engines, especially in high-stakes or regulated environments.
report.tools: Watch the paper's code release and Agent Skills specifications; evaluate on ClawArena-Team, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SkillsBench. For implementation, pair multi-agent frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, or AutoGen with policy engines like Open Policy Agent or Cedar, and sandbox execution with Docker or Firecracker. These tools help turn learned authorization signals into enforceable least-privilege controls.
